boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Independence record (October 22, 1864) in Price's Missouri Expedition [September-October 1864]. The same day's crossing of the Big Blue by Shelby is part of the Byram's Ford record (MO026) and is not added here; the night fighting toward the Big Blue and the October 23 fighting are context. Campaign-wide marches, recruiting, destruction, returns and multi-action loss totals are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. The frozen side-specific numerical strength bounds are blank (missing_numeric_strength). No figure in this pass is adopted as a simultaneous opening force.

claims.value: The frozen force field reads Provisional cavalry division and Fagan and Marmaduke's divisions; the live field reads zero. Britton says Pleasonton's division had four brigades under Brown, McNeil, Sanborn and Winslow, each with a section of 3-inch rifles, and that McNeil's and Sanborn's brigades made the attack on Cabell with Brown and Winslow following against Marmaduke. Price says Cabell's brigade was sent to drive the pursuers back and Marmaduke's division formed the rear.
claims.rationale: Unit identifications only; no count for either side. None is adopted as a matched opening strength. The live zero is not measured absence.

claims.value: The frozen and live results read Confederate victory. Britton says Pleasonton's charge broke Cabell's line, took two guns and 400 prisoners, and drove Marmaduke back toward the Big Blue by night; Price says Cabell was struck in the flank and Marmaduke was driven steadily back until late at night. NPS says Pleasonton occupied Independence but Marmaduke then pressed him back and held him.
claims.rationale: Retain the original result and engagement interval; later movements and campaign contribution are different measures. No new probabilities or individual causal credit.

open_questions: Pleasonton's (No. 13), Brown's, McNeil's, Sanborn's, Winslow's and Catherwood's reports and Clark's and Greene's reports remain deferred.

Rosecrans's, Pleasonton's and Curtis's reports, the subordinate Union and Confederate reports in Volume XLI Part 1, the organization of Price's army (No. 89), Maclean's itinerary (No. 90), the Price Court of Inquiry, Hinton's 1865 Rebel Invasion of Missouri and Kansas, maps and returns remain deferred.

NPS/CWSAC is one family (the NPS battle page plus the frozen Arnold rows). Wiley Britton's The Civil War on the Border, volume II (Putnam, 1899) is a retrospective history by a Union participant; by its preface the larger operations are based mainly on the published official reports, so it is not independent of the Price report family. Price's September 19 and November 2 dispatches and his December 28, 1864 report (Official Records Series I, Volume XLI, Part 1, No. 88) are one family of interested Confederate accounts. The Official Records volume is a shared container, not an additional witness. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
